standard.title: Places of Significance, Perspectives and Experiences
standard.description: the places of significance where Australians fought, their perspectives and experiences, including the Gallipoli campaign, the Western Front and the Middle East
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can describe historical turning points and examine the experiences and perspectives of different groups in earlier historical periods (AC9HH8K03, AC9HH8K04). They have not yet examined the specific geography of WW1 theatres, the nature of industrialised warfare (trench warfare, military technology), or the contrast between experiences on the Western Front and in the Middle East.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify the major theatres where Australians fought (Gallipoli, Western Front, Middle East), describe the conditions and experiences of soldiers in each theatre, investigate the difficulties of trench warfare and the development of military technology, and compare and contrast the different experiences of foot soldiers on the Western Front and Light Horse in the Middle East.

nodes.label: Geography of WW1 theatres — where Australians fought
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the major theatres where Australians fought and locate key battlefields on a map — Gallipoli, the Western Front (Somme, Pozières, Passchendaele, Fromelles, Bullecourt, Villers-Bretonneux) and the Middle East (Sinai, Gaza, Beersheba).
nodes.minimum_width: Students name and locate the three major theatres (Gallipoli, Western Front, Middle East) and identify at least two named battlefields in each.
nodes.typical_width: Students locate all named battlefields on a map of Europe and the Middle East; describe the approximate dates and sequence of Australian involvement in each theatre; explain why the Western Front was the dominant theatre for Australian forces after 1915; connect theatre geography to strategic objectives.
wider: Investigate the strategic logic of the Gallipoli campaign — the Allied plan to knock Ottoman Turkey out of the war and open a supply route to Russia — to understand why Australia was fighting in the Dardanelles rather than France
Map the movement of the ANZAC forces through the Sinai and Palestine campaign chronologically, tracing the shift from defensive to offensive operations
nodes.hinge_reason: Geographic grounding is the prerequisite for all subsequent nodes. Students who cannot locate the theatres and battlefields cannot make sense of the conditions and experiences described in N2–N3 — 'trench warfare' only makes sense in the Western Front context, and the Light Horse experience only makes sense in the Palestinian desert context. Theatre geography sets up the comparison in N4.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly conflate all WW1 combat with Gallipoli or treat the Western Front as a single undifferentiated place. Explicit map work — locating theatres and individual battlefields — builds the spatial scaffold the comparison node (N4) requires.

success_criteria: Identifies and locates the three major theatres on a map
Names at least two specific battlefields in each theatre

nodes.label: The Gallipoli campaign — context, experience and significance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the Gallipoli campaign — its objectives, what happened, and the experience of ANZAC soldiers — and explain why it holds particular significance in Australian national memory.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the strategic objective of the Gallipoli landings, describe the conditions experienced by ANZAC soldiers (cliff terrain, entrenched positions, heat, disease, supply difficulties), and note the eventual evacuation and its significance.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the April 25 landing and its immediate difficulties; the eight-month stalemate at Anzac Cove; key events (the August Offensive, Battle of Lone Pine, Chunuk Bair); the evacuation; the high casualty rates relative to tactical gain; explain why Gallipoli — a military failure — became a foundational national story.
wider: Examine the experience from the Ottoman Turkish perspective using sources such as Atatürk's 1934 statement about the ANZACs — how has Turkey's own commemoration of Gallipoli evolved?
Investigate specific personal accounts — letters, diaries, photographs — of Gallipoli to ground the general experience in individual voices, applying source analysis skills (AC9HH9S03)

response_modes.reason: Students commonly have prior cultural knowledge of Gallipoli (ANZAC Day, family stories, media) that is often heroic and oversimplified. Examining it as a specific military operation with a specific experience — rather than purely as national myth — prepares the ground for the commemoration debates in AC9HH9K12.

success_criteria: Describes the strategic objective of the Gallipoli campaign and what happened
Describes the conditions experienced by ANZAC soldiers at Gallipoli

nodes.label: The Western Front — trench warfare and military technology
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the conditions of trench warfare on the Western Front and explain how the development of military technology shaped the nature of warfare — including tanks, aeroplanes, and chemical weapons.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe trench warfare conditions (mud, disease, stalemate, artillery bombardment, 'going over the top'), identify at least two military technologies introduced during WW1, and explain how each affected the nature of fighting.
nodes.typical_width: Students describe the trench system architecture (front-line, support, reserve trenches; no-man's land); explain why the Western Front became a stalemate (artillery superiority, machine guns, barbed wire, the difficulty of territorial advance); describe the role of tanks in attempting to break the stalemate; aeroplanes in reconnaissance and later air combat; poison gas (chlorine, phosgene, mustard gas) and its particular psychological and physical effects; connect technology development to the human casualty scale.
wider: Investigate the Battle of the Somme's first day (1 July 1916) as a case study in the gap between pre-battle confidence and actual battlefield conditions — examining how commanders assessed success and failure
Examine the development of gas warfare from both attacker and defender perspectives — how masks and defensive measures evolved in response, connecting scientific and military thinking
Explore how the Western Front experiences are represented in literature and art — Wilfred Owen, C.E.W. Bean's accounts — and what these sources reveal about soldier perspectives
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the nature of Western Front warfare — particularly the combination of industrial-scale artillery and the inability of infantry to exploit artillery gains before defenders recovered — is the prerequisite for understanding the casualty scale and the turning points in AC9HH9K10. Students who cannot explain the stalemate logic cannot understand why the Russian Revolution and American entry (N-level turning points in K10) were so significant.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Literary and artistic representation of trench warfare (Owen, Bean, official war art) offers rich cross-disciplinary connection and source analysis opportunity. The technology-stalemate analysis connects to AC9HH9K10's turning points questions and demands genuine analytical thinking about cause and consequence.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe the Western Front as 'terrible' without understanding the structural reasons for stalemate — why couldn't either side advance? Making the artillery-gap-consolidation-cycle explicit as the mechanism explains both the casualty scale and the appeal of tanks as a solution.

Encountering the Western Front experience through multiple source types — personal accounts, photographs, statistics, technological analysis — builds a more complete picture than any single source provides.

success_criteria: Describes trench warfare conditions on the Western Front and explains why stalemate developed
Identifies at least two military technologies introduced during WW1 and explains how each affected the nature of fighting

nodes.label: Comparing experiences — Western Front and Middle East
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare and contrast the different experiences of Australian soldiers on the Western Front and in the Middle East, identifying key differences in terrain, warfare type, conditions, and the nature of the fighting.
nodes.minimum_width: Students produce a comparison of the two theatres on at least three dimensions: terrain/environment, type of warfare (trench vs mobile), conditions faced, and the role of different military units (infantry vs Light Horse).
nodes.typical_width: Students compare the two theatres systematically — the mud and stalemate of Flanders vs the heat, mobility and cavalry charges of Palestine; the infantry-centred warfare of the Western Front vs the mounted warfare and greater mobility of the Light Horse; the strategic objectives in each theatre; the casualty rates and types; examine soldier accounts from both theatres to ground the comparison in perspective; explain why both theatres feature in Australian national memory though the Western Front claimed more Australian lives.
wider: Examine the Battle of Beersheba as a case study in the contrast — the famous Light Horse charge as a moment of mobility warfare in sharp contrast to the Western Front's static character — investigating whether it has been mythologised
Compare how Australian soldiers wrote about their experiences in the two theatres — do accounts from the Middle East and Western Front have different emotional or descriptive registers?
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The comparison demands genuine analytical synthesis across multiple dimensions — terrain, warfare type, human experience, national memory — making this a rich higher-order node where width investment produces meaningful depth. Beersheba as a case study integrates historical skills with the conceptual content.

response_modes.reason: This node requires students to coordinate the specific knowledge from N2 (Gallipoli/Middle East) and N3 (Western Front) into a structured comparison — applying both content knowledge and historical comparison skills simultaneously.

success_criteria: Compares the Western Front and Middle East theatres on at least three dimensions including terrain and type of warfare
Explains the different roles of infantry (Western Front) and Light Horse (Middle East) and what each reveals about the respective theatres
